Who plays both?
A class in Mumbai has 40 students. 24 play cricket, 20 play football and 4 play neither. Aarav and Zoya disagree about how many play both.
Aarav
24 + 20 = 44. The class has 40, so 44 − 40 = 4 must play both.
Zoya
The 4 who play neither are outside both circles. So 40 − 4 = 36 play a sport, and 44 − 36 = 8 play both.
Aarav is right (4 students)
Take the class size away from the two counts added together, and you get the overlap.
Try it with 4 in both. Then 20 play only cricket and 16 play only football. 20 + 4 + 16 = 40, which leaves nobody outside the circles. But 4 students play neither.
Zoya is right (8 students)
First take away the 4 who play neither. The overlap is how far 44 goes past the 36 who are left.
Yes. 16 play only cricket, 8 play both and 12 play only football. 16 + 8 + 12 + 4 = 40.
Neither. It is 24 − 20 = 4.
The overlap is the difference between the two counts.
24 − 20 compares the sizes of the two circles. It says nothing about how much they overlap.
First find how many are inside the circles. The overlap is how far the two counts add up past that.

How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?
Your class has 30 students. The teacher asks everyone in the cricket team to stand up. How does each student know whether to stand?

Each student checks one rule: am I in the cricket team? The answer is yes or no, never maybe. A rule like that sorts the whole class into in and out. The days of the week that start with T work the same way. Tuesday and Thursday are in, and nothing else is.

On paper, write the group inside curly brackets: {Tuesday, Thursday}. Order does not matter, so {Thursday, Tuesday} is the same group. Writing a day twice adds nothing. Now draw a box around everything you could have chosen from, all seven days.
Why must the rule be so strict? Try the rule "tall students". Is a student of 150 cm tall? People will disagree, so nobody can count the group. A clear yes-or-no rule is what makes counting possible.

A collection with a clear rule for what is in it is called a set. Each thing in it is a member, also called an element. The sign ∈ means "is a member of", so Tuesday ∈ {Tuesday, Thursday}. The box of everything you could choose from is the universal set, written ξ.
Let ξ be the whole numbers from 1 to 10. Find the even numbers in ξ. Test each number against the rule: is it even? 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 pass. So the set is {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, and it has 5 members.
It is tempting to count a repeated thing twice. The letters of the word MUMBAI make the set {M, U, B, A, I}. That is 5 members, not 6. M appears twice in the word, but once in the set.
ξ is the whole numbers from 1 to 20. How many members does the set of multiples of 3 in ξ have?
A set is a collection with a yes-or-no rule, and each thing in it counts once.
In a class of 30, some students play cricket and some play football. A few play both. You draw one circle for each sport. Where do the students who play both go?

Each name goes in one place on the page. Cricket only goes in one circle, and football only in the other. A student who plays both has to be inside both circles at once. So the circles must overlap, and those students go in the shared middle.

In the figure, move the sliders to 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both. Circle A is cricket and circle B is football. The middle holds the 7 who play both. The green box around everything holds all 30 students.
Why overlap the circles rather than draw them apart? A student who plays both needs a spot that is inside both circles. Two circles drawn apart have no such spot. Overlapping them makes one.

A drawing of sets as circles inside a box is a Venn diagram. The middle part, in A and in B, is the intersection, written A ∩ B. Everything in A or B or both is the union, written A ∪ B. To tell them apart, ∪ looks like the letter U, for union. ∩ is the same shape upside down.

Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. A ∩ B holds what is in both lists, so A ∩ B = {3, 4}. A ∪ B holds everything in either list, once each, so A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Check: 3 and 4 appear once in the union, not twice.

It is tempting to read "A or B" as one of them but not both. In sets, "or" always includes the middle. A student who plays cricket and football is in A ∪ B. Leave the middle out and your count comes up short.
A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and B = {4, 8, 12}. How many members does A ∪ B have?
The intersection is what two sets share, and the union is everything in either one, counted once.
A survey of 30 students finds that 18 play cricket and 15 play football. But 18 + 15 = 33, which is more than the whole class. Did the survey go wrong?

Nothing went wrong. The 7 students who play both were counted with the cricket players, and again with the football players. Count them once and 18 + 15 − 7 = 26 play at least one sport. That leaves 30 − 26 = 4 who play neither.

In the figure, keep 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both. Read the three parts inside the circles: 11 play cricket only, 7 play both and 8 play football only. 11 + 7 + 8 = 26. The 4 in the green box outside the circles make the total 30.

Why take the overlap away exactly once? Adding the two circles' counts adds the middle twice, once with each circle. Every other part is added once. Taking the middle away once leaves every student counted exactly once.

Write n(A) for the number of members of A. The rule is n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Everything in the universal set that is not in A is the complement of A, written A′. The 4 students outside both circles make up (A ∪ B)′.
In a group of 40 people, 25 like tea, 22 like coffee and 10 like both. How many like neither? First the union: 25 + 22 − 10 = 37 like at least one. Then the complement: 40 − 37 = 3 like neither.

The tempting slip is to forget the people outside the circles. In the tea survey, 37 is not the whole group. The 3 who like neither still belong to the 40. Before you finish, check that the four parts add up to the total: 15 + 10 + 12 + 3 = 40.
In a class of 32, 20 take art, 15 take music and 6 take both. How many take neither?
Add the two circles, take away the overlap once, and whatever is left of the total sits outside both.
A dosa stall offers three fillings: potato, cheese and onion. You may choose any mix of them, or none at all. How many different dosas can you order?

List them by size. There is 1 plain dosa with nothing. There are 3 with one filling. There are 3 with two fillings: potato and cheese, potato and onion, cheese and onion. There is 1 with all three. That is 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8 dosas.
On paper, go through the fillings one at a time. Potato is in or out: 2 choices. Cheese is in or out, which doubles it to 4. Onion is in or out, which doubles it to 8.

Why does each new filling double the count? Every order you had before now comes in two versions. One leaves the new filling out and one puts it in. No order is lost and none is counted twice. So 3 fillings give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 orders.

Each order is a subset of {potato, cheese, onion}: a set whose members all come from the bigger set. We write {potato, cheese} ⊆ {potato, cheese, onion}. The plain dosa is the empty set, { }, which is a subset of every set. The set of all the subsets is the power set. A set with 3 members has 2³ = 8 subsets.
List the subsets of {red, blue}. Each colour is in or out. Both out gives { }. One in gives {red} and {blue}. Both in gives {red, blue}. That is 4 subsets, and 2² = 4, so the power set has 4 members.
Two subsets are easy to forget: the empty set and the whole set itself. A list for {red, blue} that stops at {red} and {blue} has only 2 of the 4. Check your count against 2 × 2 = 4.
A set has 4 members. How many subsets does it have?
A subset is any choice of members from a set, and each new member doubles the number of choices.
Riya says: if a number ends in 0, it is in the 5 times table. Dev says: if a number is odd, it is in the 3 times table. Who is right?

Test Dev's claim. 3 is odd, and it is in the 3 times table. 9 works too. Then try 5. It is odd, but it is not in the 3 times table. That one number sinks the claim. Riya's claim survives every number you try: 10, 20, 70, 1,000.

On paper, draw a circle for the numbers that end in 0. Draw the 5 times table as a bigger circle around it. The small circle sits completely inside the big one. Riya's claim says exactly that: no number ending in 0 is outside the big circle.

Why can a hundred numbers that fit never prove Riya right? A claim about every number is a promise with no exceptions. Numbers that fit cannot rule out a later one that does not. One exception breaks the promise at once. To prove Riya right you need a reason. A number ending in 0 is 10 × something, and 10 = 2 × 5.

A claim of the form "if this, then that" is an if-then statement, written p ⇒ q. The arrow is read "implies". In Dev's claim, p is "the number is odd" and q is "it is in the 3 times table". A case where p is true and q is false is a counterexample. 5 is a counterexample to Dev's claim.

Is this true: if a number is a multiple of 4, then it is even? A counterexample would be a multiple of 4 that is odd. But 4 × anything = 2 × (2 × anything), and 2 × anything is even. No counterexample can exist, so the statement is true.

It is tempting to flip the arrow. If it is raining, then the road is wet. That does not mean every wet road had rain. A burst pipe wets the road too. Turning p ⇒ q round gives a new claim, and it can be false while p ⇒ q is true.
Find a counterexample to this claim: if a number is a multiple of 3, then it is odd. Give the smallest one above 0.
An if-then statement is a promise, and one counterexample is enough to break it.
A sign at a swimming pool in Mumbai says: if you swim here, you have a pass. A guard at the gate meets someone with no pass. What can the guard be sure of?
That person is not swimming here. If they were swimming, they would have a pass. So no pass means no swimming. The guard knows this without looking at the pool.

On paper, draw the swimmers as a small circle inside a bigger circle of pass holders. Put a dot outside the pass circle for the person at the gate. The dot is outside the swimmers' circle too, because that circle sits inside the pass circle.

Why do the two sentences say the same thing? They describe the same picture: swimmers inside pass holders. "If swimming, then pass" reads it from the inside out. "If no pass, then not swimming" reads it from the outside in. One cannot be true without the other.
From p ⇒ q you can make "if not q, then not p". This is called the contrapositive. It is true whenever p ⇒ q is true, and false whenever p ⇒ q is false.

Write the contrapositive of: if a number is a multiple of 10, then it ends in 0. Swap the two parts and put "not" in front of each. If a number does not end in 0, then it is not a multiple of 10. Test it on 25: it does not end in 0, and 25 is not in the 10 times table.

The tempting slip is to add the two "not"s and forget to swap. "If you do not swim here, you have no pass" is a different claim. It is false, because many pass holders stay dry. Both parts must swap, and both must get a "not".
A rule says: if it rains, the match is cancelled. Today the match was not cancelled. Did it rain? Answer yes or no.
Swap the two parts and say not to both, and you get the same promise read from the outside in.

The 4 students outside both circles play neither sport. You could say they are not in "cricket or football". You could also say they are not in cricket and not in football. Do the two descriptions always pick the same students?

To be outside the union, a student must miss cricket and also miss football. Missing only one sport is not enough. So "not cricket-or-football" and "not cricket and not football" pick out the same 4 students.
In the figure, look at the green box outside both circles. On paper, shade everything outside A, then everything outside B. The part you shaded twice is exactly the part outside both circles.

Why must this work for every pair of sets, not only this class? Each member is in A or not, and in B or not. That makes only four kinds of member. Check the two descriptions on all four kinds and they agree every time. Four kinds cover every case.

A table that checks a claim on every mix of true and false is a truth table. The rule you found is one of De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. The other law says (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. In both, the dash moves inside and ∪ and ∩ swap.
Check the second law with ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4}, A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}. A ∩ B = {2}, so (A ∩ B)′ = {1, 3, 4}. A′ = {3, 4} and B′ = {1, 4}, so A′ ∪ B′ = {1, 3, 4}. The two sides match.

It is tempting to move the dash inside and keep the sign, as if (A ∪ B)′ were A′ ∪ B′. Test it on the class of 30 with 7 in both. A′ ∪ B′ holds everyone who misses at least one sport. That is 30 − 7 = 23 students, not the 4 who play neither.
ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}. How many members does A′ ∩ B′ have?
Outside A or B means outside both, so a dash over a bracket turns ∪ into ∩.

Two trains from Dadar
Fast trains leave Dadar every 12 minutes. Slow trains leave every 18 minutes. Both leave together at 8:00 AM. Kabir and Meera disagree about when they next leave together.
Kabir
Multiply the two gaps. 12 × 18 = 216, so it is 216 minutes later.
Meera
Count on in 12s and in 18s. The first number in both lists is 36, so it is 36 minutes later.
Kabir is right (216 minutes)
To find when two things next happen together, multiply the two gaps.
The trains do leave together after 216 minutes. But they have already left together five times before that. The first time is after 36 minutes.
Meera is right (36 minutes)
The 12s go 12, 24, 36. The 18s go 18, 36. The first number in both lists is 36.
Yes. 36 = 3 × 12 and 36 = 2 × 18, so both trains leave at 8:36 AM.
Neither. It is 6 minutes.
6 is the biggest number that divides into both 12 and 18.
6 does divide into both. But after 6 minutes neither train has left again. The answer must be a number that 12 and 18 both divide into.

Why minus times minus is plus
Multiplying by −1 turns you round on the number line.
Two about-turns leave you facing the way you started.
A shop owes its supplier ₹50 on each of 3 bills. The supplier cancels all 3 bills. Is the shop better or worse off, and by how much?
Losing a debt is a gain. Take away 3 debts of ₹50 and the shop is ₹150 better off. That is what (−3) × (−50) = +150 says: three lots of owing fifty, removed.

Stand at 0 on a number line, facing the positive numbers. Multiplying by −1 means turn around. Turn around once and you face the negative numbers. Turn around twice and you face forward again. In the figure, set the turns to 0, 1 and 2 and watch the arrow.

Why must the answer be positive? Follow this pattern. 3 × (−2) = −6. 2 × (−2) = −4. 1 × (−2) = −2. 0 × (−2) = 0. Each answer is 2 more than the one before. Keep going, and the pattern forces (−1) × (−2) = +2 and (−2) × (−2) = +4. Any other answer would break the pattern.

Numbers with a direction, like +5 and −5, are called directed numbers. The rule has two parts. Same signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer. Dividing follows the same rule, because dividing undoes multiplying.
Work out (−4) × 6 ÷ (−3). First the size: 4 × 6 = 24, and 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Now the signs. There are two minus signs, which is two about-turns. You finish facing forward, so the answer is +8.

The rule is for multiplying and dividing only. −3 − 4 is not +7. It is −7, because you start at −3 and move 4 further left. The saying “two minuses make a plus” tempts you to use the rule where it does not belong. When you add or subtract, walk it on the number line.
Multiplying by a negative number is an about-turn, so two of them leave you facing forward.
A class of 24 can line up in equal rows in many ways. A class of 23 cannot, however you try. What makes 23 so awkward?
24 splits into equal rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 or 12. 23 only works as one long row. Some numbers break into smaller pieces. Others refuse to break at all.

Break 60 into two pieces that multiply to make it: 6 × 10. Break those again. 6 is 2 × 3 and 10 is 2 × 5. Now nothing breaks any further. You are left with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Drawn on paper, this looks like a tree with 60 at the top.

Start a different way: 60 = 4 × 15. Then 4 is 2 × 2 and 15 is 3 × 5. You get 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 again. Whichever way you break a number, you finish with the same unbreakable pieces. They are the number's ingredients list, and every number has exactly one.

A number that divides exactly into another is called a factor. 6 and 10 are factors of 60. A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is a prime number. The unbreakable pieces of 60 are its prime factors, and the drawing is a factor tree. 1 is not prime, because it has only one factor.
Write 84 as a product of prime factors. 84 = 2 × 42. 42 = 2 × 21. 21 = 3 × 7. Every piece is now prime. So 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Check by multiplying back: 4 × 21 = 84.

It is tempting to stop too early. 84 = 4 × 21 is true, but 4 and 21 can both still break. Keep going until every piece is prime. A second trap is to think every odd number is prime. 9, 15 and 21 are odd, and none of them is prime.
Write 90 as a product of prime factors.
Every whole number bigger than 1 is either prime or built from primes in exactly one way.
A florist has 24 roses and 36 marigolds. She wants identical bunches with no flowers left over. What is the largest number of bunches she can make?
The number of bunches must divide exactly into 24 and into 36. 2 bunches work. So do 3, 4, 6 and 12. The biggest that works is 12, with 2 roses and 3 marigolds in each bunch.

Use the ingredients lists. 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Both lists contain two 2s and one 3. Those shared pieces multiply to 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. In the figure, set the two numbers to 24 and 36 and read the blue bar.

Why do the shared pieces give the biggest answer? A number divides into 24 only if all its pieces are in 24's list. To divide into both numbers, its pieces must be in both lists. Take every shared piece and you have the biggest such number.

The biggest number that divides into both is the highest common factor, or HCF. Now turn the question round. The numbers in a times table are called multiples. 24, 48 and 72 are multiples of 24. The smallest number in both times tables is the lowest common multiple, or LCM. For 24 and 36 it is 72, the amber bar.

Two buses leave the depot together. One leaves every 12 minutes and the other every 18. When do they next leave together? The multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36. The multiples of 18 are 18, 36. They meet at 36 minutes, so the LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. With prime factors: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. Take each prime the most times it appears in either list. That gives 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.

The tempting shortcut for the LCM is to multiply the two numbers. 12 × 18 = 216 is a common multiple, but it is not the lowest. Multiplying counts the shared pieces twice. In fact HCF × LCM always equals the two numbers multiplied together. Here 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.

The HCF is built from the prime pieces two numbers share, and the LCM from every piece either one needs.
You forward a message to 2 friends. Each of them forwards it to 2 more, and so on. How many people receive it in the 10th round?
Each round doubles the one before: 2, 4, 8, 16. Round 10 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is 1,024 people. Writing ten 2s is slow and hard to check. We need a shorthand.
Write the count of 2s as a small raised number: 2¹⁰. Now look at 2³ × 2². Written out, that is (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2). Count the 2s. There are five, so 2³ × 2² = 2⁵.
Multiplying joins two chains of 2s into one longer chain, so the counts add. Dividing cancels 2s from the chain, so the counts subtract. 2⁵ ÷ 2² removes two of the five 2s and leaves 2³.

2¹⁰ is called a power of 2. The 2 is the base and the small 10 is the index. The plural of index is indices. The counting shortcuts are the laws of indices. To multiply powers of the same base, add the indices. To divide, subtract them.

Simplify 3⁴ × 3² ÷ 3³. Multiplying adds: 4 + 2 = 6, giving 3⁶. Dividing subtracts: 6 − 3 = 3, giving 3³. And 3³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Now try 5² ÷ 5². Subtracting the indices gives 5⁰. But any number divided by itself is 1. So 5⁰ = 1.
There are two traps. First, 2³ is not 2 × 3. It is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Second, the laws need the same base. 2³ × 3² is two different chains, so work out each one: 8 × 9 = 72.
Write 7³ × 7⁵ as a single power of 7.
A power counts how many times a number is multiplied by itself, so multiplying powers adds the counts.
A square garden has an area of 49 square metres. How long is each side? Now make the area 2 square metres. How long is each side this time?

For 49, you need a number that multiplies by itself to give 49. That is 7. For 2, try 1.4. 1.4 × 1.4 = 1.96, which is a little too small. Try 1.5. 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25, which is too big. The side is somewhere between.
Zoom in. 1.41 × 1.41 = 1.9881. 1.42 × 1.42 = 2.0164. So the side is between 1.41 and 1.42. Each extra decimal place gets closer to 2. None of them ever lands on it exactly.

Could some fraction land on it exactly? Suppose one did, written in its lowest terms. Then top × top would equal 2 × bottom × bottom. That makes top × top even, so top is even. Write top as 2 × something, and the same line shows that bottom is even too. But a fraction in its lowest terms cannot have both parts even. So no fraction works. This argument is more than 2,000 years old.

The number that multiplies by itself to give 49 is the square root of 49, written √49 = 7. Numbers that can be written as fractions are called rational. Numbers that cannot, like √2, are called irrational numbers. Their decimals never end and never repeat.
Between which two whole numbers does √50 lie? 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64. 50 is between 49 and 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8. It is only a little above 7, because 50 is only a little above 49.
√16 is 4, not 8. Halving is tempting because it also makes a number smaller. Check by multiplying back: 4 × 4 = 16, but 8 × 8 = 64.
√30 lies between two whole numbers. What is the smaller one?

What fraction is 0.999…?

Kym eats 2 slices of a pizza cut into 4 equal slices. Aarav has a pizza of the same size, cut into 8 equal slices, and eats 4. Who ate more?

They ate the same amount: half a pizza each. Cutting every slice in two doubles the number of slices and doubles how many you eat. The amount of pizza does not change. So 2/4 and 4/8 are two names for one amount.
Draw a bar and split it into 4 equal parts. Shade 2 of them. Now draw a line through the middle of every part. The bar has 8 parts and 4 are shaded. The shaded length has not moved.

Why does this work? Multiplying the top and the bottom by 2 is multiplying by 2/2. And 2/2 is 1 whole. Multiplying by 1 never changes an amount. Dividing the top and the bottom by the same number undoes it, so that is safe too.

The top number of a fraction is the numerator and the bottom number is the denominator. Fractions that name the same amount, like 2/4 and 4/8, are equivalent fractions. Divide the top and the bottom by their highest common factor and you reach the simplest form. For 2/4 and 4/8 that is 1/2.
Write 18/24 in its simplest form. The HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4. So 18/24 = 3/4. Check: 3 and 4 share no factor except 1, so you cannot go further.

It is tempting to add the same number to the top and the bottom. Try it: 1/2 would become 2/3. But half a pizza is not two thirds of a pizza. Adding changes the amount. Only multiplying or dividing both parts keeps it the same.
Write 24/36 in its simplest form.
Multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number gives a new name for the same amount.
Kym has 3 1/4 metres of ribbon. She cuts off 1 2/3 metres to wrap a gift. How much ribbon is left?

Quarters and thirds are pieces of different sizes, so you cannot take one from the other yet. Cut both into twelfths. A quarter is 3 twelfths and a third is 4 twelfths. Now every piece is the same size, and you can count them.

Think of 3 1/4 as 3 whole metres and 1 quarter. Each whole metre is 4 quarters, so that is 13 quarters. In the same way, 1 2/3 is 5 thirds. In twelfths, 13 quarters is 39 twelfths and 5 thirds is 20 twelfths.

Why twelfths? The new denominator must be in the 4 times table and in the 3 times table. The lowest common multiple of 4 and 3 is 12. Any common multiple would work, but the lowest keeps the numbers small.

A denominator that both fractions can share is a common denominator. Here it is 12. A fraction whose top is bigger than its bottom, like 13/4, is an improper fraction. A whole number with a fraction beside it, like 3 1/4, is a mixed number.

Work out 3 1/4 − 1 2/3. Write both as improper fractions: 13/4 and 5/3. Give both the common denominator 12: 39/12 and 20/12. Take away the numerators: 39 − 20 = 19, so the answer is 19/12. 12 twelfths make 1 whole, which leaves 7 twelfths. The ribbon left is 1 7/12 metres.

The tempting way is to take away the tops and the bottoms separately. For 3/4 − 1/3 that gives 2/1, which is 2. But you started with less than 1 whole, so 2 cannot be right. The denominator names the size of the piece. It is not something you take away.
Work out 2 1/2 − 1 2/3. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
To add or take away fractions, first cut them into pieces of the same size, then count the pieces.
A jug holds 4 litres of lassi. Each glass takes 2/3 of a litre. How many glasses can you fill?

Dividing asks how many times one amount fits into another. Start by counting thirds. Each litre holds 3 thirds, so 4 litres hold 12 thirds. Each glass uses 2 of them. 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so you can fill 6 glasses.

Draw 4 bars for the 4 litres and cut each into 3 equal parts. That makes 12 parts. Circle them in groups of 2, and you get 6 groups. In the figure, set the whole number to 4 and the bottom of the fraction to 3. Read the amber line.
Look at what you did. You multiplied 4 by 3 to count the thirds. Then you divided by 2 to make the groups. Multiplying by 3 and dividing by 2 is the same as multiplying by 3/2. So 4 ÷ 2/3 = 4 × 3/2.

Turn a fraction upside down and you get its reciprocal. The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. Multiplying fractions is the short part: multiply the numerators, then multiply the denominators. So 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8, which is half of three quarters.

Work out 1 1/2 ÷ 3/8. Write 1 1/2 as the improper fraction 3/2. The reciprocal of 3/8 is 8/3, so work out 3/2 × 8/3. Multiply the numerators and the denominators: 24/6, which is 4. Check with the meaning. Four pieces of 3/8 make 12/8, and 12/8 is 1 1/2.

Dividing does not always make a number smaller. 4 ÷ 2/3 = 6, which is bigger than 4. That feels wrong until you remember the question: how many small pieces fit? A second trap is flipping the wrong fraction. Only the one you divide by gets flipped.

A floor tile is 0.3 m long and 0.2 m wide. Is its area 0.6 square metres, or 0.06?
0.3 is 3 tenths and 0.2 is 2 tenths. 3 × 2 = 6. But tenths times tenths are hundredths, so the area is 6 hundredths. That is 0.06 square metres, ten times smaller than 0.6.
Draw a square 1 m by 1 m and cut it into a 10 by 10 grid. That makes 100 small squares. The tile reaches 3 squares one way and 2 the other. It covers 6 small squares out of 100.

As fractions, 0.3 × 0.2 is 3/10 × 2/10. Multiply the numerators to get 6. Multiply the denominators to get 100. The answer is 6/100. Each digit after a decimal point brings one more division by 10 into the answer.

The positions after the decimal point are called decimal places. 0.3 has one decimal place and 0.06 has two. To multiply decimals, multiply them as whole numbers first. Then give the answer as many decimal places as the two numbers had between them.

Work out 4.5 ÷ 0.15. Dividing by a decimal is awkward, so change the question. Multiply both numbers by 100 to get 450 ÷ 15. The answer does not change, for the same reason that equivalent fractions are equal. 45 ÷ 15 = 3, so 450 ÷ 15 = 30. Check: 30 × 0.15 = 4.5.

Multiplying does not always make a number bigger. 8 × 0.5 = 4, because 0.5 of something is half of it. And dividing by a number less than 1 makes it bigger: 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16. Ask how many halves fit into 8.
Work out 0.4 × 0.06.
Multiply decimals as whole numbers and then place the point. To divide by a decimal, scale both numbers until you divide by a whole number.
A cricket ground counts a crowd of 32,846. The newspaper prints 33,000. Has the newspaper made a mistake?
No. The first two digits carry almost all the information. 33,000 is the nearest thousand to 32,846, and it is easier to remember. The newspaper kept the digits that matter most and rounded the rest.
Mark 32,000 and 33,000 on a number line. 32,846 sits between them, much closer to 33,000. The halfway mark is 32,500. Anything at or past halfway rounds up.
Now take a tiny number: 0.004718 kg of saffron. The zeros at the front only hold the digits in place. They vanish if you write the mass as 4.718 g. The digits that measure anything start at the 4.

The digits that carry the size of a number are its significant figures. Count them from the first digit that is not zero. 32,846 to 2 significant figures is 33,000, and 0.004718 is 0.0047. Decimal places are different: they are counted from the decimal point.

Round 0.03064 to 3 significant figures. The first significant figure is the 3. The zero after the 3 counts, because it sits between measured digits. So the three figures are 3, 0 and 6. The next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so the 6 stays. The answer is 0.0306.

There are two traps. First, 0.0306 to 2 decimal places is 0.03, which throws most of the number away. Decimal places and significant figures are different counts. Second, keep the size. 32,846 to 2 significant figures is 33,000, not 33. The zeros hold the place of each digit.
Round 0.05093 to 2 significant figures.
Significant figures are counted from the first digit that is not zero, so they work for huge and tiny numbers alike.
Share ₹1 equally among 4 friends and each gets ₹0.25. Share ₹1 among 3 friends and the calculator shows 0.3333333. What went wrong with 3?

Nothing went wrong. Divide 1 by 3 by hand. 10 tenths shared among 3 is 3 each, with 1 tenth left over. That 1 tenth becomes 10 hundredths, and the same step happens again. The remainder is always 1, so the 3s never stop.
Now divide 1 by 7 by hand. The remainder at each step can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. After at most six steps, one of them must come back. From then on the digits repeat: 1 ÷ 7 = 0.142857142857…

Why does 1/4 stop when 1/3 does not? A decimal that stops is a fraction over 10, 100 or 1,000. Those denominators are built only from the primes 2 and 5. 1/4 fits, because it is 25/100. But no power of 10 is a multiple of 3, so 1/3 can never stop.

A decimal that stops, like 0.25, is a terminating decimal. A decimal whose digits repeat for ever, like 0.333…, is a recurring decimal. The three dots mean the pattern goes on. Some books put a dot over the repeating digits instead.

Write 0.333… as a fraction. Ten lots of it are 3.333…, and one lot is 0.333…, with the same tail of digits. Take one lot from ten lots and the tails cancel, so nine lots are exactly 3. The number is 3/9, which is 1/3. Now try 0.3636…, where two digits repeat. Write x for the number, so that 100x = 36.3636… and the tails match again. Subtract x and 99x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11. In the figure, set the repeating digits to 36 and follow the three rows.

0.3 and 0.333… are different numbers. 0.3 is 3/10, and 0.333… is 1/3, which is a little more. If you cut a recurring decimal short, you have rounded it. A second trap: when two digits repeat, multiplying by 10 does not line the tails up. Multiply by 100.

Draw a bar of 3 equal boxes for Kym. Under it, draw a bar of 5 boxes of the same size for Aarav. The 8 boxes together hold ₹320, so each box holds ₹40. In the figure, set the parts for A to 3 and the parts for B to 5.

Why add the 3 and the 5 first? The money is shared among all the parts, not among the two people. Once you know what 1 part is worth, each share is a multiplication. Kym gets 3 × ₹40 = ₹120 and Aarav gets 5 × ₹40 = ₹200. Check: ₹120 + ₹200 = ₹320.

A comparison like 3 to 5 is called a ratio, and it is written 3 : 5. It does not say how much each person gets. It says how the amounts compare. You can simplify a ratio the way you simplify a fraction: divide every part by a common factor. So 6 : 10 is the same ratio as 3 : 5.

Share ₹4,500 among three cousins in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. There are 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts. One part is ₹4,500 ÷ 9 = ₹500. The shares are 2 × ₹500 = ₹1,000, 3 × ₹500 = ₹1,500 and 4 × ₹500 = ₹2,000. Check: the three shares add up to ₹4,500.

The tempting step is to divide by one of the numbers in the ratio, such as ₹320 ÷ 3. But 3 is not the number of parts. There are 8. A second trap is to read 3 : 5 as the fraction 3/5. Kym gets 3 parts out of 8, which is 3/8 of the money.
Meera and Zoya share 42 stickers in the ratio 2 : 5. How many stickers does Zoya get?
To share in a ratio, add the parts, find what one part is worth, then multiply.
A recipe for 4 people needs 300 g of paneer. Kym is cooking for 10 people. How much paneer does she need?
Find the amount for 1 person first. 300 g ÷ 4 = 75 g each. Then multiply by the number of people: 10 × 75 g = 750 g. Going through one turns every question of this kind into the same two steps.

Draw two number lines, one above the other. The top line counts people: 0, 1, 4 and 10. The bottom line shows the paneer: 0 g, 75 g, 300 g and 750 g. Each number on the bottom line is 75 times the number above it.

Why is this allowed? Each person eats the same amount, so the paneer grows in step with the people. Multiply the people by 2.5 and the paneer is multiplied by 2.5 too. You can check: 4 × 2.5 = 10 and 300 × 2.5 = 750.

Finding the value of one first is called the unitary method. Two amounts are in direct proportion when multiplying one by a number multiplies the other by the same number. Here the paneer is directly proportional to the people. The amount for one, 75 g, stays the same all the way along.

5 notebooks cost ₹180. What do 8 cost? One notebook costs ₹180 ÷ 5 = ₹36. So 8 notebooks cost 8 × ₹36 = ₹288. Check that the answer is sensible: 8 is less than double 5, and ₹288 is less than double ₹180.

A common slip is to divide the wrong way round and work out 5 ÷ 180. Say what you want in words first. Rupees for each notebook means rupees ÷ notebooks. A second trap: not everything doubles together. A taxi charges ₹50 to start and ₹15 for each kilometre. A 2 km trip costs ₹80 and a 4 km trip costs ₹110, not ₹160.
6 pencils cost ₹45. How much do 10 pencils cost?
Find what one is worth, then multiply by how many you need.
4 painters can paint the school hall in 6 days. The head teacher hires 8 painters instead. Will the job take 12 days?
No. More painters share the same work, so the job takes less time, not more. The hall needs 4 × 6 = 24 days of one painter's work. Shared among 8 painters, that is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 days.

Think of the hall as 24 squares of wall. One painter paints one square a day. 4 painters cover 4 squares a day and finish in 6 days. 8 painters cover 8 squares a day and finish in 3 days. The 24 squares never change.

Why multiply here, when the last section divided? Ask what stays the same. For the paneer, the amount for each person stayed the same, so you divided to find it. For the painters, the whole job stays the same, so you multiply to find it.

Two amounts are in inverse proportion when multiplying one by a number divides the other by the same number. Double the painters and the time halves. Multiply the two amounts together and the answer is always the same. Here it is 24.

A sack of rice feeds 12 hostel students for 10 days. How long does it feed 15 students? The sack holds 12 × 10 = 120 days of rice for one student. Shared among 15 students, it lasts 120 ÷ 15 = 8 days. Check that the answer is sensible: more students, so fewer days.

The tempting step is the unitary method in its usual order: 10 ÷ 12, then × 15. That gives 12.5 days, which says more students make the rice last longer. Before any sum, ask one question. If this number goes up, does the other go up or down?
A tank of water lasts 20 goats for 9 days. How many days does it last 30 goats?
When more of one thing means less of the other, find the total first, then share it out.
A pair of shoes costs ₹2,000. In June the price goes up by 20%. In the July sale it comes down by 20%. Is it back to ₹2,000?

No. The rise is 20% of ₹2,000, which is ₹400, so the price becomes ₹2,400. The cut is 20% of ₹2,400, which is ₹480. The sale price is ₹1,920. The second 20% was taken from a bigger amount, so it took off more.

Draw a bar of 10 boxes for ₹2,000. A 20% rise adds 2 boxes, which makes 12. Now cut the new bar into 10 equal pieces and take 2 of them away. Each piece is bigger than an old box, so you take away more than you added.

There is a shorter way to see it. After a 20% rise you have 100% + 20% = 120% of the price. 120% is 120/100, which is 1.2. So a 20% rise is the same as multiplying by 1.2. After a 20% cut you have 80% left, so you multiply by 0.8. Both changes together: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.

The one number you multiply by to make a percentage change is called the percentage multiplier. For a rise, add the percentage to 100% and write the result as a decimal. For a fall, take it away from 100%. A 5% rise has the multiplier 1.05 and a 30% fall has the multiplier 0.7.

A phone costs ₹15,000 and its price rises by 8%. The multiplier is 1.08. ₹15,000 × 1.08 = ₹16,200. Now go back to the ₹2,000 shoes, which went up 20% and then down 20%. The multiplier for both changes together is 0.96. ₹2,000 × 0.96 = ₹1,920, which matches. 0.96 is 96%, so the two changes make a 4% fall. In the figure, read the green line.

There are two traps. First, a 5% rise is × 1.05, not × 1.5 and not × 0.05. Multiplying by 0.05 finds the 5% on its own. Second, percentages in a row do not add. Two rises of 10% are not a rise of 20%. They make 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, which is a 21% rise.
A bag costs ₹800. Its price is cut by 15%. What is the new price?
A percentage change is one multiplication, and changes in a row multiply.
In a sale, everything is 20% off. A kurta costs ₹1,200 in the sale. What did it cost before?

It is tempting to add 20% of ₹1,200, which gives ₹1,440. But the 20% was taken off the old price, not the sale price. The sale price is 80% of the old price. So 80% is ₹1,200, 10% is ₹150 and 100% is ₹1,500.
Draw a bar of 10 boxes for the old price. Cross out 2 boxes for the 20% off. The 8 boxes left hold ₹1,200, so each box holds ₹150. All 10 boxes hold ₹1,500.
The sale multiplied the old price by 0.8. To undo a multiplication, you divide. ₹1,200 ÷ 0.8 = ₹1,500. Adding 20% back does not undo it, because that multiplies by 1.2. And 0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96, not 1.

Finding the amount before a percentage change is called a reverse percentage. Work out the multiplier for the change, then divide the new amount by it. Dividing by the multiplier always takes you back to the start.

After a 12% rise, a month's rent is ₹5,600. What was the old rent? The multiplier for a 12% rise is 1.12, so work out ₹5,600 ÷ 1.12. Multiply both numbers by 100 to get 560,000 ÷ 112, which is 5,000. The old rent was ₹5,000. Check forwards: ₹5,000 × 1.12 = ₹5,600.

The trap is to take the percentage of the wrong amount. 12% of ₹5,600 is ₹672, and ₹5,600 − ₹672 = ₹4,928. Test that answer by going forwards. ₹4,928 × 1.12 = ₹5,519.36, which is not ₹5,600. The 12% in the question was 12% of the old rent, the number you are looking for.
After a 10% rise, a cinema ticket costs ₹330. What did it cost before the rise?
To undo a percentage change, divide by its multiplier.
Kym's grandmother puts ₹1,000 in a bank that pays 8% interest a year. She leaves it there for 20 years. Kym says the bank adds ₹80 a year, so it will grow to ₹2,600. Is she right?

Only if the bank pays on the first ₹1,000 each year and nothing more. Most banks do better than that. They add the interest to the account, and the next year they pay 8% on the new, bigger amount. Year 1 ends on ₹1,080. Year 2 adds 8% of ₹1,080, which is ₹86.40, not ₹80.

Make a table with one row for each year, starting from ₹1,000. Each row is the row above × 1.08: ₹1,080, then ₹1,166.40, then ₹1,259.71. The steps get bigger every year, because each one is 8% of a bigger number.

Each year multiplies by 1.08, so 20 years multiply by 1.08 twenty times. A calculator gives that as about 4.66. So the ₹1,000 becomes about ₹4,661. That is far more than ₹2,600, and the only difference is interest earning interest.

Interest paid only on the starting amount is simple interest. It adds the same sum every year. Interest paid on the growing total is compound interest, and growth of this kind is compound growth. It multiplies by the same number every year. A quick guide is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly percentage to estimate the years needed to double.

₹20,000 is saved at 5% compound interest for 2 years. The multiplier is 1.05 each year. ₹20,000 × 1.05 = ₹21,000, and ₹21,000 × 1.05 = ₹22,050. The interest earned is ₹2,050. Simple interest would have paid 2 × ₹1,000 = ₹2,000. Now use the rule of 72 on the ₹1,000 that Kym's grandmother saved at 8%. 72 ÷ 8 = 9, so her money doubles about every 9 years. In the figure, set the interest rate to 8% and read the amber lines.

The trap is to treat compound growth as adding. 8% a year for 20 years is not 160% in total. It is × 1.08 twenty times, which is a rise of about 366%. The same trap works against you with a loan. A debt at 24% a year doubles in about 3 years.
₹2,000 is saved at 5% compound interest a year. How much is in the account after 2 years?
Compound growth multiplies by the same number each year, so the growth itself grows.

At the school canteen a samosa costs ₹15 and a cup of chai costs ₹10. Kym buys 3 samosas and 2 chais, and Aarav buys 5 samosas and 1 chai. Is there one rule that prices every order?
Every bill is worked out the same way. Kym pays 3 × ₹15 + 2 × ₹10 = ₹65. Aarav pays 5 × ₹15 + 1 × ₹10 = ₹85. Only the two counts change from one order to the next.
Make a table with a column for samosas, a column for chais and a column for the bill. Each row is one order. The ₹15 and the ₹10 sit in every row. The counts are the only boxes that change.

Why use a letter? Write s for the number of samosas and c for the number of chais. Then every bill is 15 × s + 10 × c rupees. One line of maths now stands for every row of the table, even orders nobody has placed yet.

A letter that stands for a number that can change is called a variable. Here s and c are variables. Numbers, variables and signs joined into a rule, such as 15s + 10c, make an expression. We write 15s for 15 × s and leave out the × sign. An expression has no = sign.
Pens cost ₹12 each and notebooks cost ₹30 each. An order of p pens and n notebooks costs 12p + 30n rupees. For 4 pens and 2 notebooks, that is 12 × 4 + 30 × 2 = 48 + 60 = ₹108.

The tempting slip is to read 15s as two digits side by side. With s = 2, that would make 152. In algebra, a number written next to a letter is multiplied by it, so 15s is 15 × 2 = 30. A second trap is to think s means samosa. It means the number of samosas.
A bus ticket costs ₹20 for an adult and ₹10 for a child. Write an expression for the cost, in rupees, of a adults and k children.
A variable stands for a number that can change, and an expression is a rule built from it.
The canteen bill for s samosas and c chais is 15s + 10c rupees. What does Meera pay for 4 samosas and 3 chais?
Put 4 where the s is and 3 where the c is. Then 15s + 10c becomes 15 × 4 + 10 × 3. That is 60 + 30, so Meera pays ₹90.
Think of each letter as an empty box. Write the bill as 15 × ( ) + 10 × ( ). Then drop each number into its own box and work out the sum.
Why keep the boxes as brackets? A letter stands for its whole number, sign and all. So when t = −3, t² means (−3) × (−3), which is 9. Without the bracket, −3² reads as −(3 × 3), which is −9.
Putting numbers in place of the letters is called substitution. Write each number in a bracket as you substitute it. Then work in the usual order: brackets, powers, × and ÷, and last of all + and −.
Find 3x² − 2y when x = −2 and y = 5. Write it with brackets: 3 × (−2)² − 2 × (5). The power comes first: (−2)² = 4. So the value is 3 × 4 − 10 = 12 − 10 = 2.

One slip is to square only the 2 and keep the minus outside, which gives 3 × (−4) − 10 = −22. Another is to work out 3 × (−2) first and then square it, which gives 36 − 10 = 26. Powers come before multiplying.
Find the value of a² + 4a when a = −3.
Substitute each number in a bracket, then work out powers before you multiply.

A pack of pencils costs p rupees and an eraser costs e rupees. On Monday Kym buys 3 packs and 2 erasers. On Friday she buys 4 packs and 1 eraser. Her spending is 3p + 2e + 4p + e. Can it be written in fewer pieces?
The packs can be counted together, and so can the erasers. 3 packs and 4 packs make 7 packs, and 2 erasers and 1 eraser make 3. So her spending is 7p + 3e.
Sort the shopping into two piles. The pencil pile holds 3 packs and then 4, which is 7. The eraser pile holds 2 and then 1, which is 3. A pack and an eraser never share a pile.
Why not join 7p and 3e into 10 of something? They count different things. Test it with prices. If p = 20 and e = 5, then 7p + 3e = 140 + 15 = 155. But 10p would be 200 and 10e would be 50.

The parts of an expression joined by + or − are the terms of the expression. In 7p + 3e − 4, the terms are 7p, 3e and −4. The number in front of a letter is its coefficient, so the coefficient of p is 7. Terms with exactly the same letters are like terms. Only like terms can be added together.
Simplify 5a + 3b − 2a + b. The a terms are 5a and −2a, which make 3a. The b terms are 3b and b, and b on its own has coefficient 1. They make 4b. So 5a + 3b − 2a + b = 3a + 4b.

The tempting step is to add every number and write 7ab. But a and b count different things. Watch the signs too: the minus in −2a belongs to that term, so 2a is taken away. And x and x² are not alike. When x = 3, x is 3 but x² is 9.
Simplify 6x + 2y − x + 5y.
Only like terms can be added, so collect each letter's terms on their own.
A school orders 4 kits. Each kit holds a geometry box at ₹65 and a ruler at ₹15. Kym works out 4 × 80. Aarav works out 4 × 65 + 4 × 15. Who is right?
Both are. Kym gets 4 × ₹80 = ₹320, and Aarav gets ₹260 + ₹60 = ₹320. Four kits hold four boxes and four rulers, so you can count whole kits or count the pieces.

Draw a rectangle 4 squares tall and 80 squares long. Its area is 4 × 80. Draw a line down it 65 squares from the left. The two pieces have areas 4 × 65 and 4 × 15, and together they fill the rectangle.

The same cut works when one length is a letter. 4(x + 3) means 4 × (x + 3). A rectangle 4 tall and x + 3 long splits into a piece 4 by x and a piece 4 by 3. So 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12, whatever number x stands for.
Writing 4(x + 3) as 4x + 12 is called expanding brackets, or multiplying out. The number outside multiplies every term inside the bracket. It works for a minus sign too: 5(2y − 1) = 10y − 5.

Expand and simplify 3(2x + 5) − 2(x − 4). The first bracket gives 6x + 15. The second has −2 outside, so it gives −2x + 8, because −2 × −4 = +8. Collect like terms: 6x − 2x = 4x and 15 + 8 = 23. The answer is 4x + 23.

The common slip is to multiply only the first term, so 3(2x + 5) becomes 6x + 5. Draw 3(2x + 5) as a rectangle 3 tall, and the piece for the 5 is 3 tall as well, so it is 15. The other slip is a sign. −2(x − 4) is −2x + 8, not −2x − 8.
Expand and simplify 4(2x + 3) + 3(x − 2).
The number outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it, sign and all.
A tiled floor is 6 tiles wide and holds 42 tiles, so it is 7 tiles long. Another floor is also 6 tiles wide, and it holds 12x + 18 tiles. How long is that floor?
Run expanding brackets backwards. 12x is 6 × 2x, and 18 is 6 × 3. So 12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3), and the floor is 2x + 3 tiles long.
Draw the rectangle with its side of 6 marked. Cut it into two pieces with areas 12x and 18. Each piece is 6 tall, so their lengths are 2x and 3. The whole length is 2x + 3.
Why take out 6 and not 2? Both 2 and 3 divide each term too. But 12x + 18 = 2(6x + 9), and 6x and 9 still share a 3. Taking out the highest common factor leaves nothing more to take out.

Writing an expression as a number or letter times a bracket is called factorising. Find the HCF of the terms, write it outside a bracket, and divide each term by it. A letter can be part of the HCF too: 5x² + 15x = 5x(x + 3).

Factorise 20p²q + 8pq. The HCF of 20 and 8 is 4. Both terms have at least one p and one q. So the HCF of the terms is 4pq. 20p²q ÷ 4pq = 5p and 8pq ÷ 4pq = 2. The answer is 4pq(5p + 2). Check by expanding: 4pq × 5p = 20p²q.

The usual slip is to stop too soon. 20p²q + 8pq = 2p(10pq + 4q) is true, but 2 and q are still common to both terms in the bracket. Another slip is to lose a term. When a whole term is the HCF, it leaves 1 behind: 3x + 3 = 3(x + 1).
Factorise 14y − 21.
To factorise, take the HCF outside a bracket, then check by expanding.
A square photo is 6 cm by 6 cm. A border makes it 3 cm longer and 2 cm taller, so it is 9 cm by 8 cm. Kym says the new area is 6 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 42 cm². Is she right?
No. The new photo is 9 cm by 8 cm, so its area is 72 cm². Kym counted the old photo and the small corner, but she left out two strips. One strip is 3 by 6 and the other is 6 by 2.

Draw the 9 by 8 rectangle and cut it into four pieces. They hold 6 × 6 = 36, 3 × 6 = 18, 6 × 2 = 12 and 3 × 2 = 6, which make 72. In the figure, set the side to 6, the first number to 3 and the second number to 2.
Now let the side of the square be x. The four pieces are x², 3x, 2x and 6. So (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 3x + 2x + 6, which is x² + 5x + 6. Each part of one bracket multiplies each part of the other.

An expression like x² + 5x + 6, where the highest power of x is 2, is called a quadratic expression. To expand two brackets, multiply each term of one by each term of the other. That makes four products, and the middle two are like terms.
Expand (x + 5)(x − 2). Draw a grid with x and 5 along the top and x and −2 down the side. The four boxes hold x², 5x, −2x and −10. The middle pair make 5x − 2x = 3x. So (x + 5)(x − 2) = x² + 3x − 10.

The famous trap is to write (x + 3)² as x² + 9. But (x + 3)² is (x + 3)(x + 3), and the square has two strips of 3x as well as its corners. So it is x² + 6x + 9. In the figure, set both numbers to 3 and look at the two blue strips. Test with x = 4: 7² = 49, and 16 + 24 + 9 = 49.
Expand and simplify (x + 4)(x + 6).
Multiply each term in one bracket by each term in the other, then collect the like terms.
Work out 53² − 47² with no calculator. Squaring both numbers takes a long time. Is there a quicker way?

Try smaller numbers first. 5² − 3² = 25 − 9 = 16, and (5 − 3) × (5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 as well. 7² − 2² = 49 − 4 = 45, and 5 × 9 = 45. Each time, one square take away the other equals the gap times the total.
Draw a 5 by 5 square and cut a 3 by 3 square from one corner. The L-shape left over holds 16 small squares. Cut the L into two strips and lay them end to end. They make a rectangle 2 wide and 8 long.

The same cut works for any two numbers. A square of side a with a corner of side b cut away leaves an L-shape. It always rearranges into a rectangle a − b wide and a + b long. So a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).

Kym says: I thought of a number, multiplied it by 3 and then added 5. I got 26. Aarav finds her number without guessing. How does he do it?
He runs her steps backwards. Her last step was adding 5, so he takes 5 away: 26 − 5 = 21. Before that she multiplied by 3, so he divides by 3: 21 ÷ 3 = 7. Her number was 7.
Draw a row of boxes joined by arrows: start, then × 3, then + 5, then 26. Under it, draw the arrows pointing the other way: 26, then − 5, then ÷ 3. The start box fills in as 7.
Why go back in reverse order? The last thing done is the first thing to undo. You take off your shoes before your socks. Check the answer forwards: 7 × 3 = 21 and 21 + 5 = 26.

Kym's puzzle, with n for her number, is 3n + 5 = 26. A statement that two expressions are equal is called an equation. It is true for some values of n only. Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing. They are inverse operations.
Aarav's puzzle is n ÷ 4 − 2 = 3. Undo the last step first: 3 + 2 = 5. Then undo the dividing: 5 × 4 = 20. His number was 20. Check: 20 ÷ 4 − 2 = 3.

The tempting slip is to undo the steps in the order they were done. Dividing 26 by 3 first gives 8⅔, and 8⅔ − 5 = 3⅔. Test it forwards: 3⅔ × 3 + 5 = 16, not 26. Another slip is to repeat a step. 26 + 5 does not undo adding 5.

Solve an inequality like an equation. On a number line, < and > get an open circle, and ≤ and ≥ a filled dot. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round.
Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount smaller. 0.4 of something is less than all of it.
Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount bigger. Scale both numbers up until you divide by a whole number: 7 ÷ 0.25 is 700 ÷ 25.
A percentage change is one multiplication. A 15% rise is × 1.15 and a 15% fall is × 0.85. To go back to the old amount, divide by the multiplier. Changes in a row multiply.
Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to write one number: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Pick the form that makes the sum shortest.
A length in metres is 100 times as many centimetres. An area has two lengths, so multiply by 100 twice: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². A volume has three, so 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.
Put both amounts in the same unit first. Then divide every part of the ratio by a common factor until no more will go.
Add the parts, find what one part is worth, then multiply for each share. If you are told a difference and not the total, match it to the difference in parts.
In direct proportion, both amounts are multiplied by the same number. In inverse proportion, one is multiplied and the other is divided, so multiplying them together always gives the same answer.

Same signs make a positive and different signs make a negative, so (−3) × (−2) = 6 and 6 ÷ (−3) = −2, and a minus sign stays with its number through every step. Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number turns the sign round: −x < 2 becomes x > −2.

Undo the last step first and do the same to both sides: for x/2 + 3 = 8, take 3 from both sides to get x/2 = 5, then multiply by 2 to get x = 10. An inverse function f⁻¹ makes those undo steps; it is not 1 ÷ f.
The number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside it: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12. A squared bracket is two brackets, so (x + 2)² = (x + 2)(x + 2) = x² + 4x + 4, not x² + 4.

The HCF is the biggest number that divides both, and the LCM is the smallest number both divide into: for 4 and 10, the HCF is 2 and the LCM is 20, not 4 × 10 = 40. Cancel a fraction by the HCF so nothing common is left, as in 10/15 = 2/3.

Squaring multiplies a number by itself, so 5² = 5 × 5 = 25, not 10, and a square root undoes it: √25 = 5. In a right-angled triangle, square the two shorter sides, add, then take the square root: 3² + 4² = 25, so the longest side is 5.
Add or subtract fractions only once they share a denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, never 2/5. Turn a mixed number into an improper fraction first, so 1 1/2 is 3/2.

Look at the digit after the last one you keep and round up if it is 5 or more, so 2.367 to 2 decimal places is 2.37, not 2.36. Significant figures start at the first digit that is not zero: 0.005281 to 2 significant figures is 0.0053.

Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left, so 0.47 × 100 = 47, and a recurring decimal never stops, so 10 × 0.333… take away 0.333… is exactly 3. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 until it is whole: 12 ÷ 0.3 = 120 ÷ 3 = 40.
Ask what one of something is worth: if 4 pens cost £6, one pen costs 6 ÷ 4 = £1.50, and the amount you share out goes first. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer, so 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4.

Find one part first: to share 45 in the ratio 4 : 5, there are 9 parts, so one part is 5 and the shares are 20 and 25. If more workers do the same job, it takes less time: 2 workers taking 6 hours means 1 worker takes 12 hours.

A percentage change is one multiplication: a 30% decrease is × 0.7 and a 5% increase is × 1.05. Two changes multiply, so up 40% then down 40% is × 1.4 × 0.6 = × 0.84, and to undo a change you divide by its multiplier.

Change every length to the same unit before you calculate: 1 m = 100 cm, so 3.2 m = 320 cm. An area scales by the square of the length factor, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², and doubling every length makes an area 4 times as big.

A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, so base 6 cm and height 4 cm give 12 cm², and a slanted side is never the height. Use the radius in πr², and add every edge for a perimeter: a quarter circle of radius 2 cm has perimeter π + 4.

Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°, and an exterior angle of a polygon is 180° take away the interior angle, so an interior angle of 108° has exterior angle 72°. A back-bearing is the bearing plus 180°, or minus 180° if that passes 360°: the back-bearing of 050° is 230°.

The midpoint averages the x-coordinates and then the y-coordinates, keeping x first: the midpoint of (1, 2) and (5, 10) is (3, 6). Gradient is change in y ÷ change in x, and a perpendicular gradient flips it and changes its sign, so 2/3 becomes −3/2.

Check the mirror line or centre before you move: reflecting (3, 4) in the y-axis gives (−3, 4), and a 90° turn clockwise about the origin takes (x, y) to (y, −x). To enlarge about a centre, multiply the step from the centre to the point, then add it back on: (3, 2) from centre (1, 1) by scale factor 3 is (7, 4).

List every outcome so each one is equally likely: a coin and a spinner numbered 1 to 3 give H1, H2, H3, T1, T2 and T3, six outcomes. When order does not matter, a pair like AB is the same as BA, so count it once.

The total is the group you are picking from at that moment. If 1 of 10 sweets is eaten, the next pick is out of 9, and if you are told the person wears glasses, the total is only the people who wear glasses.

Class width is the upper boundary take away the lower one, and frequency density is frequency ÷ class width: 10 ≤ x < 40 has width 30, so frequency 60 gives density 2. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, not the largest value minus the smallest.
Add or subtract the top numbers, then the bottom numbers: (2, 5) − (3, 1) = (−1, 4). To go from P to Q, go back to O and then out again, so PQ = −p + q.
Sequences start at n = 1, so test a rule by putting n = 1 and n = 2 back in: for 2, 7, 12, … the rule 5n − 3 gives 2, then 7. Counting from 3 to 6 including both ends gives 4 numbers, not 3.
